species
family
order

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In basidiomycetes, the dikaryotic structure formed after plasmogamy ultimately gives rise to the basidium.
Statement II: In basidiomycetes, the basidia are arranged in fruiting bodies called ascocarps.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: In basidiomycetes, plasmogamy is by fusion of two somatic cells of different strains. The resulting structure is dikaryotic, which ultimately gives rise to the basidium. Karyogamy and meiosis take place in the basidium, producing four basidiospores. The basidia are arranged in fruiting bodies called basidiocarps; ascocarps are the fruiting bodies of ascomycetes.
steps: Statement II: basidia lie in basidiocarps, not ascocarps; false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biological Classification', Kingdom Fungi (Basidiomycetes)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (term) with List-II (meaning as given in NCERT).

List-I:
A. Identification
B. Nomenclature
C. Classification
D. Systematics

List-II:
I. Grouping into convenient categories based on some easily observable characters
II. Describing an organism correctly so that we know to what organism a name is attached
III. A study that takes into account evolutionary relationships between organisms
IV. Naming of an organism according to standardised rules and criteria

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III
A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III
A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I
A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III

solution.explanation: Nomenclature (naming) is possible only when the organism is described correctly and we know to what organism the name is attached - this is identification. Nomenclature gives scientific names according to agreed principles and criteria. Classification is the process by which anything is grouped into convenient categories based on some easily observable characters. Systematics deals with the classification of organisms and takes into account evolutionary relationships between them.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap identification with nomenclature, classification with systematics, or nomenclature with classification.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'The Living World', Diversity in the Living World
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about fungi are correct?

(a) In ascomycetes, conidia on germination produce mycelium.
(b) Penicillium is a multicellular ascomycete, whereas yeast (Saccharomyces) is a unicellular one.
(c) In basidiomycetes, vegetative reproduction by fragmentation is common.
(d) Phycomycetes are found only in aquatic habitats.
(e) In ascomycetes, the conidiophores bear ascospores.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a) and (b) only
(a), (b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(b), (c) and (d) only

solution.explanation: Ascomycetes are mostly multicellular (Penicillium) or rarely unicellular (yeast, Saccharomyces). Their asexual spores, conidia, are produced exogenously on conidiophores and on germination produce mycelium; the sexual spores, ascospores, are produced endogenously in asci. In basidiomycetes asexual spores are generally not found, but vegetative reproduction by fragmentation is common. Phycomycetes occur in aquatic habitats, on decaying wood in moist and damp places, or as obligate parasites on plants.
steps: (d) false: also on decaying wood and as obligate parasites on plants
(e) false: conidiophores bear conidia; ascospores form in asci
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (c). The other combinations include (d) or (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biological Classification', Kingdom Fungi
solution.final_answer: Option C: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.question_text: In ciliated protozoans such as Paramoecium, the coordinated movement of rows of cilia causes the water laden with food to be steered into the:

options.text: gullet
contractile vacuole
pseudopodium
spore-like infectious stage

solution.explanation: Ciliated protozoans are aquatic, actively moving organisms because of the presence of thousands of cilia. They have a cavity (gullet) that opens to the outside of the cell surface. The coordinated movement of rows of cilia causes the water laden with food to be steered into the gullet.
steps: Ciliated protozoans: thousands of cilia and a gullet
Rows of cilia steer food-laden water into the gullet
solution.why_others_wrong: Pseudopodia are put out by amoeboid protozoans; an infectious spore-like stage is a feature of sporozoans. NCERT does not describe the cilia as steering food into a contractile vacuole.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biological Classification', Kingdom Protista (protozoans)
solution.final_answer: Option A: gullet

questions.question_text:

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In gymnosperms, the pollen tube carrying the male gametes grows towards the archegonia in the ovules. According to NCERT, it discharges its contents:

options.text: inside the microsporangium
near the mouth of the archegonia
on the surface of the megasporophyll, outside the ovule
into the soil, where the gametes swim to the ovule

Pollen tube grows to the archegonia
Contents discharged near the mouth of the archegonia

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following structures are diploid?

(a) The seta of a moss
(b) The megaspore mother cell in the ovule of a gymnosperm
(c) A leaf of a fern
(d) The protonema of a moss
(e) An antherozoid of a fern

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a) and (b) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (c) and (d) only

solution.concept: Haploid and diploid structures in plant groups
solution.explanation: In mosses the zygote develops into the sporophyte (foot, seta and capsule), which is diploid; the spores formed in it by meiosis give the haploid protonema. In gymnosperms the megaspore mother cell, differentiated from a cell of the nucellus, is diploid and divides meiotically. In ferns the main plant body, with its leaves, is the diploid sporophyte, while the antherozoids are produced on the haploid gametophyte.
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (b) only leaves out the fern leaf. The other combinations include the haploid antherozoid or the haploid protonema.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Kingdom', Bryophytes; Pteridophytes; Gymnosperms

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct for a fern such as Dryopteris?

(a) Its main plant body is a sporophyte differentiated into true root, stem and leaves.
(b) Its leaves are large (macrophylls).
(c) Its gametophyte needs cool, damp, shady places to grow.
(d) Its sporophyte remains attached to and nourished by the gametophyte throughout life.

(a) and (c) only
(b), (c) and (d) only

solution.explanation: In pteridophytes the main plant body is a sporophyte with true root, stem and leaves; the leaves are small (microphylls) as in Selaginella or large (macrophylls) as in ferns. The sporophyte is the dominant, independent phase, and pteridophytes form no ovules or seeds.
steps: (d) false: that is the bryophyte condition
solution.why_others_wrong: The other combinations either add (d) or (e), or leave out the true statement (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Kingdom', Pteridophytes

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In which of the following plants is the dominant, independent, photosynthetic phase haploid?

options.text: Polytrichum
Pteris
Cycas
Selaginella

solution.concept: Dominant phase in different plant groups
solution.explanation: In bryophytes such as the moss Polytrichum, the main plant body is haploid; it produces gametes and is called a gametophyte. In pteridophytes (Pteris, Selaginella) and gymnosperms (Cycas), the main plant body is the diploid sporophyte.
steps: Fern, Selaginella, Cycas: dominant phase = sporophyte (2n)
solution.why_others_wrong: Pteris and Selaginella are pteridophytes and Cycas is a gymnosperm; in all three the dominant, independent plant is the diploid sporophyte.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Kingdom', Bryophytes; Pteridophytes; Gymnosperms
solution.final_answer: Option A: Polytrichum

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following are true of members of Chlorophyceae but NOT of members of Phaeophyceae, according to NCERT's table of the divisions of algae?

(a) Chlorophyll b is present.
(b) The stored food is starch.
(c) The motile cells bear 2-8 equal, apical flagella.
(d) Cellulose is a component of the cell wall.

options.text: (a) and (b) only
(a), (c) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(b), (c) and (e) only

solution.explanation: Chlorophyceae: chlorophyll a and b; stored food starch; cell wall of cellulose; 2-8 equal, apical flagella; fresh, brackish and salt water. Phaeophyceae: chlorophyll a and c with fucoxanthin; stored food mannitol and laminarin; cell wall of cellulose and algin; 2 unequal, lateral flagella; fresh water (rare), brackish and salt water.
steps: (d) both have cellulose in the wall
(e) both occur in brackish and salt water
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (b) only misses the flagellar difference. The other combinations include (d) or (e), which are shared by both classes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Kingdom', Algae (table: divisions of algae and their main characteristics)

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
How many of the following are formed by meiosis?

(i) Spores in the capsule of a moss
(ii) The four megaspores in a gymnosperm ovule
(iii) Gemmae of Marchantia
(iv) Microspores of Selaginella
(v) Antherozoids of a fern
(vi) The zygote of a moss

solution.concept: Where meiosis occurs in plant groups
solution.explanation: Meiosis produces spores: in mosses the spores are formed within the capsule after meiosis; in gymnosperms the megaspore mother cell divides meiotically to form four megaspores; in pteridophytes, including the heterosporous Selaginella, the sporangia produce spores by meiosis in spore mother cells. Gemmae are asexual buds of the haploid thallus, antherozoids are produced in antheridia on the haploid gametophyte, and a zygote is formed by fusion of gametes - none of these by meiosis.
steps: Not by meiosis: (iii) gemmae, (v) antherozoids, (vi) zygote
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 leaves out the Selaginella microspores, forgetting that heterosporous spores also arise by meiosis. 4 counts gemmae as meiotic products, and 5 also counts the antherozoids.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Kingdom', Bryophytes; Pteridophytes; Gymnosperms
solution.final_answer: Option C: 3

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which of the following is true of the female gametophyte of BOTH Selaginella and Pinus?

options.text: It develops from a microspore.
It is retained on the parent sporophyte: for variable periods in Selaginella, and within the megasporangium in Pinus.
It is enclosed within an ovary wall.
It is the dominant, long-lived phase of the plant.

solution.explanation: In heterosporous pteridophytes such as Selaginella, the female gametophyte is retained on the parent sporophyte for variable periods, an event regarded as a precursor to the seed habit. In gymnosperms such as Pinus, the multicellular female gametophyte is retained within the megasporangium on the sporophyte.
steps: Selaginella: female gametophyte retained on parent sporophyte
Pinus: female gametophyte retained within megasporangium
solution.why_others_wrong: Female gametophytes develop from megaspores, not microspores. Neither plant has an ovary, and in both the dominant phase is the sporophyte.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Kingdom', Pteridophytes; Gymnosperms
solution.final_answer: Option B: It is retained on the parent sporophyte: for variable periods in Selaginella, and within the megasporangium in Pinus.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In both Selaginella and Pinus, the sporophylls are arranged to form strobili (cones).
Statement II: In both Salvinia and Cycas, the ovules develop into naked seeds after fertilisation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: In some pteridophytes, such as Selaginella and Equisetum, the sporophylls form compact strobili. In gymnosperms such as Pinus, sporophylls are arranged spirally along an axis to form lax or compact strobili or cones. Salvinia, however, is a heterosporous pteridophyte; it forms no ovules or seeds. Only gymnosperms such as Cycas have naked seeds.
steps: Statement II: false; Salvinia is a pteridophyte and has no seeds
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Kingdom', Pteridophytes; Gymnosperms
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (structure in a gymnosperm) with List-II (origin or composition).

List-I:
A. Pollen grain
B. Ovule
C. Female gametophyte
D. Seed

List-II:
I. Develops from one of the four megaspores
II. Develops from the ovule after fertilisation
III. Highly reduced male gametophyte developing from a microspore within the microsporangium
IV. Nucellus together with the envelopes that protect it

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I
A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II
A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

solution.explanation: Microspores develop into a highly reduced male gametophyte, the pollen grain, within the microsporangia. The nucellus, protected by envelopes, forms the ovule. The megaspore mother cell in the nucellus forms four megaspores by meiosis, and one of them develops into the multicellular female gametophyte. After fertilisation the zygote forms the embryo and the ovules develop into seeds.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap the pollen grain and the ovule, the female gametophyte and the seed, or the ovule and the female gametophyte.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Kingdom', Gymnosperms
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: After fertilisation in a flower, according to NCERT:

options.text: the ovary develops into a seed and the ovules into the fruit wall
the stigma and style develop into the fruit
the thalamus develops into the seed coat and the ovules disappear
the ovules develop into seeds and the ovary matures into a fruit

solution.concept: Fate of the ovary and ovules
solution.explanation: NCERT (gynoecium): after fertilisation, the ovules develop into seeds and the ovary matures into a fruit. The fruit is thus a mature or ripened ovary.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options reverse or misplace the fate of the ovary and ovules; NCERT gives the ovules as forming seeds and the ovary as forming the fruit.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', The Flower (gynoecium)
solution.final_answer: Option D: the ovules develop into seeds and the ovary matures into a fruit

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In insectivorous plants such as the pitcher plant and the Venus fly trap, the structures that trap insects are modified:

options.text: roots
leaves
stems
inflorescence axes

solution.explanation: Leaves are often modified to perform functions other than photosynthesis. NCERT states that the leaves of certain insectivorous plants, such as the pitcher plant and the Venus fly trap, are also modified leaves.
steps: Pitcher and Venus fly trap: modified leaves
solution.why_others_wrong: NCERT lists these structures among leaf modifications, along with leaf tendrils (pea), spines (cactus) and fleshy leaves (onion, garlic); they are not roots, stems or inflorescence axes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', The Leaf (modifications of leaves)
solution.final_answer: Option B: leaves

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In some plants such as Rhizophora growing in swampy areas, many roots come out of the ground and grow vertically upwards. These roots are called:

options.text: pneumatophores
prop roots
stilt roots
fibrous roots

solution.explanation: NCERT: in some plants such as Rhizophora growing in swampy areas, many roots come out of the ground and grow vertically upwards. Such roots, called pneumatophores, help to get oxygen for respiration.
steps: Upward-growing roots of swamp plants = pneumatophores
solution.why_others_wrong: Prop roots are the hanging supporting roots of the banyan tree, and stilt roots arise from the lower nodes of maize and sugarcane. Fibrous roots form the root system of monocots such as wheat.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', The Root (modifications of root)
solution.final_answer: Option A: pneumatophores

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In the region of maturation of a root, some epidermal cells form very fine, delicate, thread-like root hairs. According to NCERT, these root hairs:

options.text: protect the tender apex of the root
divide repeatedly to add new cells
absorb water and minerals from the soil
elongate rapidly and are responsible for growth in length

solution.explanation: Proximal to the region of elongation, cells gradually differentiate and mature (region of maturation). From this region some epidermal cells form very fine, delicate, thread-like root hairs, which absorb water and minerals from the soil.
steps: Root hairs arise in the region of maturation
solution.why_others_wrong: Protection of the apex is the job of the root cap. Repeated division is the work of the region of meristematic activity, and growth in length that of the region of elongation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', The Root (regions of the root)
solution.final_answer: Option C: absorb water and minerals from the soil

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The ovary is the enlarged basal part of a carpel.
Statement II: The style is the elongated tube that connects the ovary to the stigma.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Each carpel is made up of stigma, style and ovary. The ovary is the enlarged basal part, on which lies the elongated tube, the style. The style connects the ovary to the stigma, which is usually at the tip of the style and is the receptive surface for pollen grains.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', The Flower (gynoecium)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (part of a maize grain) with List-II (description).

List-I:
A. Scutellum
B. Coleoptile
C. Coleorhiza
D. Aleurone layer

List-II:
I. Sheath enclosing the radicle
II. Proteinaceous layer separating the endosperm from the embryo
III. One large, shield-shaped cotyledon
IV. Sheath enclosing the plumule

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II
A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

solution.explanation: In maize, the embryo is small and lies in a groove at one end of the endosperm. It has one large, shield-shaped cotyledon called the scutellum and a short axis with a plumule and a radicle. The plumule and radicle are enclosed in sheaths called the coleoptile and coleorhiza respectively. The outer covering of the endosperm separates the embryo by a proteinaceous aleurone layer.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap the two sheaths, the scutellum and the coleoptile, or the coleorhiza and the aleurone layer.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The wheat plant has a fibrous root system.
Reason (R): In wheat, the primary root is short-lived and is replaced by a large number of roots that originate from the base of the stem.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: In most dicots the primary root persists as the tap root. NCERT: in monocotyledonous plants, the primary root is short-lived and is replaced by a large number of roots. These roots originate from the base of the stem and constitute the fibrous root system, as seen in the wheat plant.
steps: Replacement of the short-lived primary root by many roots from the stem base is what forms a fibrous root system -> R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', The Root
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In which of the following pairs are BOTH structures modified leaves?

options.text: Tendrils of pea and tendrils of cucumber
Spines of cactus and thorns of Citrus
Tendrils of pea and fleshy storage leaves of onion
Green expanded petioles of Australian acacia and the flattened green structure of Opuntia

solution.explanation: Leaves are modified into tendrils for climbing (pea), spines for defence (cactus) and fleshy storage organs (onion, garlic). Stem tendrils of cucumber and pumpkin develop from axillary buds; thorns of Citrus and Bougainvillea are modified axillary buds; Opuntia has a flattened green stem.
steps: Pea tendril: leaf; onion fleshy leaf: leaf -> both leaves
Cucumber tendril, Citrus thorn and Opuntia's flattened structure: stems
solution.why_others_wrong: Each wrong pair contains one stem modification: cucumber tendrils, Citrus thorns and the flattened green structure of Opuntia are all modified stems.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', The Stem; The Leaf (modifications)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Tendrils of pea and fleshy storage leaves of onion

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following features are common to BOTH the families Fabaceae and Solanaceae, as described in NCERT?

(a) The leaves show reticulate venation.
(b) The calyx has five united sepals (gamosepalous).
(c) The leaves are stipulate.
(d) The seeds are endospermous.
(e) The inflorescence is racemose.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a) and (b) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(a) and (d) only
(b) and (e) only

solution.explanation: Fabaceae: leaves pinnately compound or simple, pulvinate leaf base, stipulate, reticulate venation; racemose inflorescence; calyx of five gamosepalous sepals; seeds non-endospermic. Solanaceae: leaves simple (rarely pinnately compound), exstipulate, reticulate venation; inflorescence solitary, axillary or cymose; calyx of five united, persistent sepals; seeds endospermous.
steps: (b) both have five united sepals: true
(e) Solanaceae inflorescence is not racemose: false
solution.why_others_wrong: The other combinations include (c), (d) or (e), each of which holds for only one of the two families.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', Description of Some Important Families (Fabaceae, Solanaceae)

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In Liliaceae the leaves are mostly basal, linear and show parallel venation, whereas in Solanaceae the leaves show reticulate venation.
Statement II: In Fabaceae, the corolla shows valvate aestivation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Leaves and aestivation in three families
solution.explanation: Liliaceae: leaves mostly basal, alternate, linear, exstipulate with parallel venation. Solanaceae: leaves alternate, simple, exstipulate, with reticulate venation. In Fabaceae the calyx shows imbricate aestivation and the papilionaceous corolla shows vexillary aestivation.
steps: Statement II: false; the corolla of Fabaceae is vexillary
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', Description of Some Important Families
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A flower has floral appendages in multiples of five, and its gynoecium occupies the highest position on the thalamus with the other parts situated below it. Such a flower is described as:

options.text: pentamerous and epigynous
pentamerous and hypogynous
tetramerous and hypogynous
trimerous and perigynous

solution.concept: Merosity and position of floral parts
solution.explanation: A flower is trimerous, tetramerous or pentamerous when its floral appendages are in multiples of 3, 4 or 5. When the gynoecium occupies the highest position and the other parts are situated below it, the flower is hypogynous and the ovary is superior.
steps: Gynoecium highest, other parts below -> hypogynous
solution.why_others_wrong: In an epigynous flower the other parts arise above the ovary (inferior ovary). Tetramerous means multiples of four and trimerous multiples of three; perigynous means the other parts arise on the rim of the thalamus at about the level of the ovary.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', The Flower
solution.final_answer: Option B: pentamerous and hypogynous

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
A flower has the floral formula ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2), with the stamens epipetalous and the ovary superior. From NCERT's description of the family to which it belongs, which of the following would you also expect in this plant?

(a) The calyx is persistent.
(b) The fruit is a berry or a capsule.
(c) The seeds are endospermous.
(d) The leaf base is pulvinate.
(e) The leaves show parallel venation.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a) and (b) only
(b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (c) and (e) only
(a), (b) and (c) only

solution.concept: Inferring family characters from a floral formula
solution.explanation: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2) with epipetalous stamens and a superior ovary is the floral formula NCERT gives for Solanaceae. In that family the calyx is persistent, the fruit is a berry or capsule, the seeds are many and endospermous, and the leaves are simple, exstipulate and reticulately veined. A pulvinate leaf base belongs to Fabaceae; parallel venation to monocots such as Liliaceae.
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (b) only leaves out the endospermous seeds. The other combinations include (d) or (e), which are not characters of Solanaceae.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', Description of Some Important Families (Solanaceae)
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the flower of pea, the stamens are diadelphous.
Reason (R): The flower of pea is zygomorphic.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Two independent features of the pea flower
solution.explanation: Stamens united into two bundles, as in pea, are diadelphous (nine united and one free, A(9)+1). The pea flower is also zygomorphic: it can be divided into two similar halves only in one vertical plane. Symmetry describes how the whole flower can be divided; it says nothing about how the filaments of the stamens are united. The two statements are separate features.
steps: Symmetry of the flower does not explain the fusion of stamens into two bundles -> R is not the explanation
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', The Flower (symmetry; androecium)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The flowers of both pea and brinjal are hypogynous.
Statement II: The gynoecium of both pea and brinjal is syncarpous.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Comparing the gynoecium of pea and brinjal
solution.explanation: In Fabaceae (pea) the ovary is superior, monocarpellary and unilocular; in Solanaceae (brinjal) it is bicarpellary, syncarpous and superior. A superior ovary means a hypogynous flower in both. Pea, with a single carpel, cannot have a syncarpous (fused carpels) gynoecium.
steps: Statement I: both have superior ovaries -> hypogynous; true
Statement II: pea is monocarpellary; false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', The Flower; Description of Some Important Families
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

Match List-I (character described in NCERT) with List-II (family or families).

List-I:
A. Placenta swollen, bearing many ovules
B. Leaf base pulvinate
C. Perianth of six tepals, often united into a tube
D. Flowers bisexual with a superior ovary

List-II:
I. Liliaceae only
II. Fabaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae

IV. Fabaceae only

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I
A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV

Liliaceae: perianth of six tepals (3 + 3), often united into a tube. In all three families the flowers are bisexual and the ovary is superior.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In Opuntia and in Australian acacia, food is synthesised largely by green structures other than a typical leaf lamina. Which statement about these structures is correct?

options.text: In both plants the green structure is a modified stem.
In both plants the green structure is a modified stipule.
In Opuntia it is the expanded petiole, whereas in Australian acacia it is a modified stem.
In Opuntia the green structure is a modified stem, whereas in Australian acacia it is the expanded petiole of the leaf.

solution.concept: Photosynthetic organs other than the lamina
solution.explanation: NCERT: some plants of arid regions modify their stems into flattened (Opuntia) or fleshy cylindrical (Euphorbia) structures that contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis. In Australian acacia the leaves are small and short-lived; the petioles expand, become green and synthesise food.
steps: Australian acacia: green, expanded petiole (part of the leaf)
solution.why_others_wrong: Only Opuntia uses a modified stem; the acacia structure is a leaf petiole. Neither is a stipule, and the last option reverses the two plants.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Morphology of Flowering Plants', The Stem; The Leaf (modifications)
solution.final_answer: Option D: In Opuntia the green structure is a modified stem, whereas in Australian acacia it is the expanded petiole of the leaf.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, the secondary or lateral meristem occurs in the mature regions of roots and shoots of many plants, particularly those that:

options.text: are grasses regenerating after grazing
are aquatic and lack vascular tissue
have no apical meristem
produce a woody axis

solution.explanation: NCERT: the meristem that occurs in the mature regions of roots and shoots of many plants, particularly those that produce a woody axis, and appears later than the primary meristem is called the secondary or lateral meristem. It is cylindrical; fascicular vascular cambium, interfascicular cambium and cork cambium are examples.
steps: Lateral meristem: mature regions of roots and shoots
Particularly in plants producing a woody axis
solution.why_others_wrong: Regeneration after grazing in grasses is due to intercalary meristems. Flowering plants are not without vascular tissue, and all have apical meristems at root and shoot tips.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Anatomy of Flowering Plants', The Tissues (meristematic tissues)
solution.final_answer: Option D: produce a woody axis

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In angiosperms, how many different kinds of elements make up the xylem and the phloem taken together, as listed in NCERT?

solution.explanation: Xylem is composed of four elements: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma. Phloem in angiosperms is composed of sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 counts only one of the two tissues. 6 leaves out the fibres of both tissues. 7 leaves out one element, such as the phloem fibres.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Anatomy of Flowering Plants', The Tissues (xylem; phloem)
solution.final_answer: Option A: 8

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The trichomes of the shoot system may be branched or unbranched, and soft or stiff.
Statement II: The waxy cuticle that covers the epidermis is absent in roots.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: On the stem, the epidermal hairs are called trichomes. They are usually multicellular, may be branched or unbranched, soft or stiff, and may even be secretory; they help prevent water loss due to transpiration. The outside of the epidermis is often covered with a waxy, thick cuticle that prevents loss of water; the cuticle is absent in roots.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Anatomy of Flowering Plants', The Tissue System (epidermal tissue system)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which of the following is found in a monocot stem but NOT in a dicot stem?

options.text: Conjoint vascular bundles
Scattered vascular bundles, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath
An epidermis forming the outermost layer
A hypodermis of a few layers of collenchymatous cells

solution.concept: Monocot stem compared with dicot stem
solution.explanation: The monocot stem has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis, a large number of scattered vascular bundles, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, and a large, conspicuous parenchymatous ground tissue. Dicot stem: bundles in a ring

solution.explanation: In both stems the xylem and phloem lie together on the same radius (conjoint), and, as in all stems, the protoxylem lies towards the centre and the metaxylem towards the periphery (endarch). The dicot stem's bundles are open and arranged in a ring; the monocot stem's bundles are closed, scattered, lack phloem parenchyma and have water-containing cavities.

(d) ring only in dicot stem: false

solution.concept: Comparing sclerenchymatous cells with companion cells
solution.explanation: Sclereids are spherical, oval or cylindrical, highly thickened dead cells with very narrow lumen. Phloem fibres are sclerenchymatous, with quite thick walls, and lose their protoplasm at maturity to become dead. Companion cells are specialised, living parenchymatous cells whose nucleus controls the sieve tubes and which help maintain the pressure gradient in them.
steps: Phloem fibres: dead at maturity, thick-walled
solution.why_others_wrong: Being living with a nucleus, and maintaining the pressure gradient, describe companion cells only. Storing resins, latex and mucilage is a function of phloem parenchyma.

epiblema, root hairs, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, conjunctive tissue, xylem, pith

solution.concept: Extent of the stele in a dicot root
solution.explanation: All tissues on the inner side of the endodermis - the pericycle, the vascular bundles (with the conjunctive tissue between xylem and phloem) and the pith - constitute the stele. The epiblema with its root hairs, the cortex and the endodermis itself lie outside it.

NCERT: in monocotyledons the vascular bundles have no cambium in them; hence they do not form secondary tissues and are referred to as closed. The absence of cambium is the reason no secondary tissues form.
steps: No cambium -> no secondary xylem or phloem -> R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Anatomy of Flowering Plants', The Tissue System (vascular tissue system)

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A transverse section of a young plant organ shows a collenchymatous hypodermis, an endodermis whose cells are rich in starch grains, and semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma above the phloem. The vascular bundles of this organ are expected to be:

radial, with exarch xylem and two to four xylem patches
conjoint and closed, scattered, each with a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath
conjoint and closed, all of nearly similar size except in the main veins

solution.explanation: A collenchymatous hypodermis, a starch sheath (endodermis rich in starch grains) and a pericycle of semi-lunar sclerenchyma patches above the phloem identify a dicot stem. Its many vascular bundles are arranged in a ring; each is conjoint, open and has endarch protoxylem.
steps: Dicot stem bundles: conjoint, open, endarch, in a ring
solution.why_others_wrong: Radial bundles with exarch xylem and 2-4 patches describe a dicot root. Scattered, closed bundles with sclerenchymatous sheaths describe a monocot stem, and bundles of nearly similar size describe an isobilateral (monocot) leaf.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Anatomy of Flowering Plants', Anatomy of Dicotyledonous and Monocotyledonous Plants (dicot stem)

matrix
lumen
perinuclear space

solution.why_others_wrong: The stroma surrounds the thylakoids. The matrix is the inner compartment of a mitochondrion, and the perinuclear space lies between the two membranes of the nuclear envelope.

freely permeable and structurally unlike that of eukaryotes
the outermost layer of the cell envelope
absent in Mycoplasma, which lacks a cell wall

Lysosome

steps: Euglenoids: pellicle instead of a cell wall

solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell: The Unit of Life', Eukaryotic Cells (plastids); Biological Classification (euglenoids)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Euglena

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, the cell cycle is divided into two basic phases. These are:

options.text: G1 phase and G2 phase
interphase and M phase
karyokinesis and cytokinesis
S phase and G0 phase

solution.concept: Two basic phases of the cell cycle
solution.explanation: The cell cycle is divided into two basic phases: interphase, the period of preparation for division (G1, S and G2), and the M phase (mitosis phase), when the actual cell division takes place.
solution.why_others_wrong: G1 and G2 are sub-phases of interphase. Karyokinesis and cytokinesis are the two parts of the M phase. G0 is a quiescent stage outside the active cycle, and S is a sub-phase of interphase.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', Cell Cycle (phases of cell cycle)
solution.final_answer: Option B: interphase and M phase

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the four stages into which karyokinesis of mitosis is divided?

options.text: Prophase
Metaphase
Telophase
Interkinesis

solution.explanation: Karyokinesis of mitosis is divided into four stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. Interkinesis is the stage between the two meiotic divisions, not a stage of mitosis.
steps: Mitotic stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
Interkinesis: between meiosis I and II
solution.why_others_wrong: Prophase, metaphase and telophase are three of the four stages of karyokinesis.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', M Phase
solution.final_answer: Option D: Interkinesis

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Meiosis II is initiated immediately after cytokinesis, usually before the chromosomes have fully elongated.
Statement II: Prophase II is a much simpler prophase than prophase I.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: meiosis II is initiated immediately after cytokinesis, usually before the chromosomes have fully elongated. Interkinesis is followed by prophase II, a much simpler prophase than prophase I.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', Meiosis (meiosis II)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Meiosis ensures that the specific chromosome number of each species is conserved across generations in sexually reproducing organisms, even though the process itself, paradoxically, results in:

options.text: doubling of the chromosome number
no change in the chromosome number of the daughter cells
the formation of diploid gametes
reduction of the chromosome number by half

solution.explanation: NCERT: the conservation of the specific chromosome number of each species across generations is achieved through meiosis, even though the process, per se, paradoxically, results in reduction of chromosome number by half. Fertilisation later restores the diploid number.
steps: Fertilisation restores it -> number conserved across generations
solution.why_others_wrong: Meiosis does not double or keep the chromosome number; it halves it, and the gametes it forms are haploid, not diploid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', Significance of Meiosis
solution.final_answer: Option D: reduction of the chromosome number by half

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
How many of the following take place during the M phase of the cell cycle?

(i) Replication of DNA
(ii) Duplication of the centriole in an animal cell
(iii) Condensation of chromosomes
(iv) Disintegration of the nuclear envelope
(v) Cytokinesis
(vi) Synthesis of proteins in preparation for mitosis

solution.concept: Events of interphase and M phase
solution.explanation: DNA replication and centriole duplication take place in the S phase, and proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis in G2 - all parts of interphase. The M phase starts with karyokinesis (condensation of chromosomes in prophase; complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope marks the start of metaphase) and usually ends with cytokinesis.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 leaves out cytokinesis, which is part of the M phase. 4 adds G2 protein synthesis or centriole duplication, and 5 adds both, though they belong to interphase.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', Cell Cycle; M Phase
solution.final_answer: Option B: 3

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Mitosis is also called equational division.
Reason (R): In plant cells, cytokinesis begins with a cell plate that forms in the centre of the cell and grows outwards.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Mitosis is called equational division because the number of chromosomes in the parent and progeny cells is the same. Separately, in plant cells the new wall begins as a cell plate formed in the centre and growing outward to meet the lateral walls. The way the cytoplasm is divided in plants has nothing to do with why mitosis keeps the chromosome number equal.
steps: A: true (same chromosome number in parent and progeny)
R is about cytokinesis in plants, not about the chromosome number -> not the explanation
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', M Phase (cytokinesis)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following take place during telophase of mitosis?

(a) The centromere of each chromosome splits.
(b) A nuclear envelope develops around each chromosome cluster at the poles.
(c) The nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform.
(d) The chromosomes decondense and lose their individuality.
(e) The chromosomes align on the metaphase plate.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (b) and (c) only
(a), (b) and (d) only
(c), (d) and (e) only
(b), (c) and (d) only

solution.explanation: At telophase the chromosomes that have reached their poles decondense and lose their individuality; the chromatin collects in a mass at each pole. A nuclear envelope develops around the chromosome clusters at each pole, forming two daughter nuclei, and the nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform. Centromeres split at anaphase, and chromosomes align on the metaphase plate at metaphase.
solution.why_others_wrong: (b) and (c) only leaves out the decondensation of chromosomes. The other combinations include (a) or (e), which belong to anaphase and metaphase.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', M Phase (telophase)
solution.final_answer: Option D: (b), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Diakinesis is marked by the formation of the synaptonemal complex.
Statement II: During diakinesis, the chromosomes are fully condensed and the meiotic spindle is assembled to prepare the homologous chromosomes for separation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: The synaptonemal complex forms in zygotene and dissolves in diplotene. Diakinesis is marked by terminalisation of chiasmata; during this phase the chromosomes are fully condensed and the meiotic spindle is assembled to prepare the homologous chromosomes for separation. By its end the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down.
steps: Statement I: false; synaptonemal complex forms in zygotene
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', Meiosis (prophase I)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A dividing cell of a diploid organism has n chromosomes, each made of two chromatids. The chromosomes are becoming compact again, and the nuclear membrane disappears by the end of the stage. The cell is in:

options.text: prophase I
prophase II
metaphase II
telophase I

solution.explanation: After meiosis I each cell has n chromosomes, each still with two chromatids. Meiosis II begins immediately; in prophase II the nuclear membrane disappears by the end of the stage and the chromosomes again become compact. In metaphase II the chromosomes align at the equator.
steps: n chromosomes with two chromatids -> after meiosis I
Chromosomes compacting, nuclear membrane disappearing -> prophase II
solution.why_others_wrong: A cell in prophase I has 2n chromosomes forming bivalents. In metaphase II the chromosomes are already aligned at the equator. In telophase I the nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear rather than disappear.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', Meiosis (meiosis II)
solution.final_answer: Option B: prophase II

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements correctly compare prophase I of meiosis with prophase of mitosis?

(a) Prophase I is typically longer and more complex than prophase of mitosis.
(b) Crossing over between non-sister chromatids occurs in both.
(c) Synapsis of homologous chromosomes takes place only in prophase I.
(d) The nuclear envelope remains intact after both of them are over.
(e) Condensation of the chromosomal material takes place in both.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a) and (c) only
(a), (b) and (e) only
(c), (d) and (e) only
(a), (c) and (e) only

solution.explanation: NCERT: prophase of the first meiotic division is typically longer and more complex than prophase of mitosis and is subdivided into leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis. Chromosomes condense in both. Synapsis (zygotene) and crossing over between non-sister chromatids (pachytene) happen only in meiosis I. The nuclear envelope breaks down at the end of mitotic prophase (its complete disintegration marks the start of metaphase) and by the end of diakinesis.
steps: (b) false: no crossing over in mitosis
(d) false: the nuclear envelope breaks down in both
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (c) only leaves out the condensation of chromosomes. The other combinations include (b) or (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', M Phase (prophase); Meiosis (prophase I)
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which of the following would NOT be seen in a cell at anaphase II of meiosis?

options.text: Homologous chromosomes paired as bivalents
Splitting of the centromere of each chromosome
Sister chromatids moving towards opposite poles
Shortening of the microtubules attached to the kinetochores

solution.explanation: Anaphase II begins with the simultaneous splitting of the centromere of each chromosome, allowing the sister chromatids to move towards opposite poles by shortening of the microtubules attached to the kinetochores. The homologous chromosomes had already separated in anaphase I, so no bivalents remain.
steps: Anaphase II: centromeres split, sister chromatids move apart, microtubules shorten
Homologues separated in anaphase I -> no bivalents
solution.why_others_wrong: Splitting of centromeres, movement of sister chromatids to opposite poles and shortening of kinetochore microtubules all happen in anaphase II.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', Meiosis (meiosis II)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Homologous chromosomes paired as bivalents

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Interkinesis is followed by a prophase that is more complex than prophase I.
Reason (R): Interkinesis, the stage between the two meiotic divisions, is generally short-lived.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: The stage between the two meiotic divisions is called interkinesis and is generally short-lived. Interkinesis is followed by prophase II, which NCERT describes as a much simpler prophase than prophase I.
steps: A: false - prophase II is much simpler than prophase I
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', Meiosis (meiosis I; meiosis II)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: At metaphase I, the chromosomes align on the equatorial plate as single, unpaired chromosomes.
Statement II: At metaphase of mitosis, both sister chromatids of a chromosome are attached to spindle fibres from the same pole.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Metaphase of mitosis and metaphase I
solution.explanation: At metaphase I, the bivalent chromosomes align on the equatorial plate, and microtubules from the opposite poles attach to the pair of homologous chromosomes. At metaphase of mitosis, one chromatid of each chromosome is connected by its kinetochore to spindle fibres from one pole and its sister chromatid to spindle fibres from the opposite pole.
steps: Statement I: false; bivalents align at metaphase I
Statement II: false; sister chromatids attach to opposite poles
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Cell Cycle and Cell Division', M Phase (metaphase); Meiosis (metaphase I)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: NCERT shows that the colour of a green leaf is due to four different pigments rather than one. The technique used to separate these leaf pigments is:

options.text: centrifugation
gel electrophoresis
paper chromatography
staining with basic dyes

solution.explanation: A chromatographic separation of the leaf pigments shows that the colour of leaves is due to four pigments: chlorophyll a (bright or blue green), chlorophyll b (yellow green), xanthophylls (yellow) and carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange). NCERT describes this separation by paper chromatography.
solution.why_others_wrong: NCERT uses paper chromatography, not centrifugation or electrophoresis, to separate the pigments; staining with basic dyes is how chromatin was named, not how pigments are separated.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Photosynthesis in Higher Plants', What is the Photosynthetic Pigment Involved in Photosynthesis?
solution.final_answer: Option C: paper chromatography

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP), the primary CO₂ acceptor in the mesophyll cells of C4 plants, is a:

options.text: 4-carbon molecule
5-carbon ketose sugar
6-carbon sugar
3-carbon molecule

solution.concept: Primary CO₂ acceptor of the C4 pathway
solution.explanation: NCERT: in the C4 pathway, the primary CO₂ acceptor is a 3-carbon molecule, phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP), present in the mesophyll cells; the enzyme is PEP carboxylase. The product is the 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid (OAA).
solution.why_others_wrong: The 4-carbon molecule is OAA, the product. The 5-carbon ketose sugar is RuBP, the acceptor of the Calvin cycle, and glucose is the 6-carbon sugar.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Photosynthesis in Higher Plants', The C4 Pathway
solution.final_answer: Option D: 3-carbon molecule

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Photosystem I and Photosystem II are named in the sequence in which they function during the light reaction.
Statement II: Each light-harvesting complex (LHC) is made up of hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: The pigments are organised into two discrete photochemical light-harvesting complexes within PS I and PS II. These are named in the sequence of their discovery, not in the sequence in which they function during the light reaction. Each LHC is made up of hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins.
steps: Statement I: false; named in order of discovery
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Photosynthesis in Higher Plants', What is Light Reaction?
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Photosynthesis is responsible for the release of oxygen into the atmosphere.
Reason (R): In the light reaction, water is split, and oxygen is released as one of the products.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Source of atmospheric oxygen from photosynthesis
solution.explanation: NCERT notes that photosynthesis is important because it is the primary source of all food on earth and is responsible for the release of oxygen into the atmosphere. This oxygen comes from the splitting of water (2H₂O -> 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻) associated with PS II in the light reaction.
steps: The O₂ that photosynthesis releases is produced by water splitting -> R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Photosynthesis in Higher Plants', Introduction; The Splitting of Water
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (component) with List-II (location or role).

List-I:
A. CF₀ of ATP synthase
B. CF₁ of ATP synthase
C. NADP reductase
D. Water-splitting complex

List-II:
I. Forms a transmembrane channel for facilitated diffusion of protons
II. Located on the stroma side of the membrane; the protons it needs are removed from the stroma
III. Protrudes on the outer surface facing the stroma; its conformational change makes the enzyme synthesise ATP
IV. Associated with PS II and located on the inner side of the membrane

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV
A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV
A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II
A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV

solution.explanation: ATP synthase has two parts: CF₀, embedded in the thylakoid membrane, forms a transmembrane channel for facilitated diffusion of protons; CF₁ protrudes on the outer surface facing the stroma, and the energy of proton movement causes a conformational change in it that makes the enzyme synthesise ATP. NADP reductase is on the stroma side, and the protons for NADPH + H⁺ are removed from the stroma. The water-splitting complex is associated with PS II on the inner side of the membrane.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap the two parts of ATP synthase, the NADP reductase with the water-splitting complex, or CF₀ with NADP reductase.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Photosynthesis in Higher Plants', The Chemiosmotic Hypothesis
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following are true of BOTH Photosystem I and Photosystem II?

(a) It is associated with the water-splitting complex.
(b) Its reaction centre is a single chlorophyll a molecule.
(c) Its light-harvesting complex has hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins.
(d) It takes part in cyclic photophosphorylation.
(e) It is located in the thylakoid membranes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (b) and (c) only
(a), (b) and (e) only
(b), (c) and (e) only
(c), (d) and (e) only

solution.concept: Common features of the two photosystems
solution.explanation: Each photosystem has a light-harvesting complex of hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins, with a single chlorophyll a molecule as the reaction centre (different in the two photosystems). The LHCs are located in the thylakoid membranes. Only PS II is associated with water splitting, and only PS I is functional in cyclic photophosphorylation.
solution.why_others_wrong: (b) and (c) only leaves out the location in the thylakoid membranes. The other combinations include (a) or (d), each true of only one photosystem.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Photosynthesis in Higher Plants', What is Light Reaction?; Cyclic and Non-cyclic Photo-phosphorylation
solution.final_answer: Option C: (b), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The reduction steps of the Calvin cycle are catalysed by RuBisCO.
Statement II: The oxygen evolved during photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: RuBisCO catalyses carboxylation, the fixation of CO₂ with RuBP to form two molecules of 3-PGA. The reduction steps that follow use ATP for phosphorylation and NADPH for reduction. The O₂ evolved in photosynthesis comes from the splitting of water, not from CO₂.
steps: Statement I: false; RuBisCO catalyses carboxylation
Statement II: false; O₂ comes from water
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Photosynthesis in Higher Plants', The Calvin Cycle; The Splitting of Water
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In a C4 plant, which option correctly pairs each carboxylating enzyme with the cells in which it fixes CO₂?

options.text: PEP carboxylase in the mesophyll cells; RuBisCO in the bundle sheath cells
RuBisCO in the mesophyll cells; PEP carboxylase in the bundle sheath cells
Both PEP carboxylase and RuBisCO in the mesophyll cells
Both PEP carboxylase and RuBisCO in the bundle sheath cells

solution.concept: Division of labour in C4 leaves
solution.explanation: In C4 plants the primary CO₂ acceptor PEP is carboxylated by PEP carboxylase in the mesophyll cells, which lack RuBisCO. The C4 acid is moved to the bundle sheath cells, broken down to release CO₂, and the CO₂ enters the Calvin cycle there. The bundle sheath cells are rich in RuBisCO but lack PEPcase.
solution.why_others_wrong: The first option reverses the two cell types. Each cell type has only one of the two enzymes, so neither 'both in one cell' option is correct.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Photosynthesis in Higher Plants', The C4 Pathway
solution.final_answer: Option A: PEP carboxylase in the mesophyll cells; RuBisCO in the bundle sheath cells

questions.question_text:
Which of the following are part of the light reactions (photochemical phase) of photosynthesis?

(a) Splitting of water
(b) Carboxylation of RuBP
(c) Formation of NADPH
(d) Regeneration of RuBP

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a) and (c) only
(a), (b) and (e) only
(c), (d) and (e) only
(a), (c) and (e) only

Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a C4 plant, the CO₂ fixed in the mesophyll cells is ultimately released in the bundle sheath cells.
Reason (R): The C4 acids (malic acid or aspartic acid) formed in the mesophyll cells are transported to the bundle sheath cells and broken down there to release CO₂ and a 3-carbon molecule.

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

There these C4 acids are broken down to release CO₂ and a 3-carbon molecule; the CO₂ then enters the Calvin cycle. The transport and breakdown of the C4 acid is how the CO₂ reaches the bundle sheath.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (feature) with List-II (plants in which NCERT describes it).

List-I:
A. The Calvin cycle as the main biosynthetic pathway
B. Initial fixation of atmospheric CO₂ by PEP carboxylase
C. 3-PGA as the first stable product of CO₂ fixation
D. Release of O₂ derived from the splitting of CO₂

I. C3 plants only

IV. Neither C3 nor C4 plants

A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I
A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV
A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV

Only C4 plants fix atmospheric CO₂ first by PEP carboxylase (first product OAA); in C3 plants the first stable product is 3-PGA. In no plant is the O₂ released derived from CO₂: it comes from the splitting of water.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which of the following does NOT take place in the bundle sheath cells of a C4 plant such as maize?

options.text: Breakdown of the C4 acid to release CO₂
Fixation of atmospheric CO₂ with phosphoenol pyruvate
Carboxylation of RuBP by RuBisCO
Reduction of PGA using ATP and NADPH

No PEPcase in bundle sheath -> PEP fixation only in mesophyll

Statement I: In the Z scheme, electrons from PS II pass downhill through the electron transport chain to the pigments of PS I, and electrons excited in the reaction centre of PS I are finally passed to NADP⁺.
Statement II: NADP reductase is located on the lumen side of the thylakoid membrane, so the protons used to reduce NADP⁺ are taken from the lumen.
